one_line: Long-running, stateful agents need controlled scenario suites, balanced scorecards and a ratchet loop, not just prompt tweaks; the speaker's case study is a game-village multi-agent system tuned by an outer auto-research loop.
summary: Erina Karati (ex-Microsoft, ex-Supercell) presents Project Paradox, a Supercell AI Innovation Lab framework for autonomous game agents with per-agent RAG memory, emotion vectors, trust/belief scores and importance-scored memories. Over long horizons the agents lost social consistency: rumors hardened into facts and sources were forgotten. The team wrapped the system in an auto-research loop, inspired by Karpathy's auto-research, that runs controlled scenarios, collects structured traces, scores behavior, proposes a small policy change, reruns, and keeps the change only if the scorecard improves and guardrails hold. The core argument is that memory alone is not enough: agents must preserve provenance (first-hand vs second-hand, confidence, verified vs uncertain) and separate raw episodic memory from current beliefs. They stress balanced scorecards over one "agent quality" metric and freezing the harness, scenarios and metrics while exposing only a small editable policy surface. The speaker explicitly says they do not yet have repeated loop results, so the talk is a method proposal with one anecdote rather than a proven benchmark.

key_ideas.idea: Long-horizon agents fail in ways single-turn evals miss
key_ideas.detail: Per-agent RAG memory and a short-term plan worked for brief play, but over longer runs a rumor about mangoes lost its source and became a stated fact, and agents forgot facts they had learned.

key_ideas.idea: Auto-research as an outer meta loop, not another agent
key_ideas.detail: The auto-research layer sits outside the simulated village. It reads full run traces, compares them with scenario ground truth, proposes a constrained protocol change, and reruns to see whether society-level behavior improved.

key_ideas.idea: Keep only changes that survive measurement (ratchet)
key_ideas.detail: Each candidate change is scored and kept only if the scorecard improves and guardrails hold; otherwise it is reverted. Rollback is treated as mandatory because one fix can damage another behavior, such as faster fact spread leaking private info.

key_ideas.idea: Use controlled scenarios with ground truth instead of letting agents wander
key_ideas.detail: Scenarios such as public-fact diffusion, rumor uncertainty and replanning after a blocked route make social behavior measurable. Open-ended simulation can look good in demos but is hard to evaluate.

key_ideas.idea: Balanced scorecard, one metric per behavior
key_ideas.detail: Metrics include reach after N steps (diffusion), source retention (provenance), uncertainty preservation and false-certainty rate (rumors), action consistency and time to re-plan (planning), and containment (privacy). Optimizing one metric alone makes agents overshare or create stale memories.

key_ideas.idea: Freeze the harness and expose only a small policy surface
key_ideas.detail: The loop may edit memory-write and retrieval policy, communication prompts, trust rules, attribution rules and planning triggers. It may not rewrite the codebase, the scenarios or the metrics, which blocks gaming the evaluation.

key_ideas.idea: Memory is not enough: store provenance and belief state
key_ideas.detail: Agents need to know whether a fact was first-hand or second-hand, verified or uncertain, and should separate raw episodic memories from current beliefs. Hedging is required when retelling uncertain claims.

key_ideas.idea: Generalizes to other stateful agents (support, personal, research, coding, workflow)
key_ideas.detail: The speaker argues that any agent whose state affects future action needs scenario suites and behavioral scorecards, with examples like policy-update provenance, commitments, citations and handoffs.

techniques.name: Controlled scenario suite with ground truth
techniques.how: Define small scenarios with known truth (for example, Agent A learns the bakery closes tomorrow; does the right agent learn it, cite the source and change its plan?). Run the agents, then score against the known answer.
techniques.when: Evaluating multi-agent or long-running stateful behavior where a single answer-quality score hides failures.

techniques.name: Balanced behavioral scorecard with guardrails
techniques.how: Measure several separate dimensions (reach, source retention, uncertainty preservation, false-certainty rate, re-plan time, containment). Accept a change only if the target metric improves and the guardrail metrics do not regress.
techniques.when: Any auto-optimization loop, so the optimizer cannot game one number.

techniques.name: Frozen-harness ratchet loop
techniques.how: Freeze the harness, scenarios and metrics. Let an outer loop edit only a small policy surface, rerun the suite, and keep the change if it passes the scorecard. Otherwise revert.
techniques.when: Self-improvement of an agent system where the optimizer might rewrite the evaluation or the codebase.

techniques.name: Structured run-trace logging
techniques.how: Log observations, conversations, memory writes, retrievals and belief updates for each run, so an outer analyzer can compare what happened with the ground truth.
techniques.when: Before building any automated analysis of agent behavior.

techniques.name: Importance-scored memory with a threshold cache
techniques.how: The LLM rates each event's importance. Memories above a threshold go into a separate high-priority store, so important context is retrieved more reliably later.
techniques.when: Long-lived agents where routine memories would crowd out critical ones.

techniques.name: Provenance and confidence tags on memories
techniques.how: Store the source, whether the info was first-hand or second-hand, a confidence level, and whether it is verified or uncertain. When the agent retells a claim, it must carry the hedge.
techniques.when: Agents that pass information between each other or answer questions about who said what.

techniques.name: Separate episodic memory from current belief
techniques.how: Keep raw episodic memories apart from a derived belief layer that holds what the agent currently holds to be true, with trust and emotion scores that the LLM updates after each interaction.
techniques.when: Agents that must track what is true, uncertain or outdated over time.

hot_takes: Memory alone (RAG) does not give long-horizon agent behavior; agents also need provenance and a separate belief state.
A single vague 'agent quality' metric hides the failures that matter; use a balanced scorecard.
Self-improvement loops should freeze the harness, scenarios and metrics, and expose only a small policy surface.
Any agent whose stored state affects future action (support, personal, research, coding, workflow) has the same problem.

relevance.why: MemoryMesh already has tiered cross-session memory with conflict resolution and provenance. The talk's point that source and first-hand vs second-hand status must survive recall applies directly.
relevance.action: Add source, first-hand/second-hand and confidence fields to MemoryMesh memory writes, then write a small scenario where a fact passes through two agents and check that the source and hedge survive retrieval.

relevance.why: EvolveCraft and SkillForge need a success signal and a way to keep only changes that help. The ratchet loop with a frozen harness and a guardrailed scorecard answers both questions.
relevance.action: Design the EvolveCraft/SkillForge success signal as a balanced scorecard with guardrail metrics. Freeze the harness and the eval set, and allow the loop to edit only the skill-selection or prompt policy.

relevance.why: ProsHarness runs long Claude Code jobs with checkpoints and loops. A frozen scenario set with a pass/fail scorecard could gate changes to its loop prompts, but the talk does not cover that setting.
relevance.action: Read the talk's ratchet and frozen-harness section, then consider a fixed regression scenario set for ProsHarness plan/critique prompts before accepting prompt edits.

relevance.why: Practical method for evaluating stateful agents: scenarios with ground truth, a multi-metric scorecard, and rollback. It is applicable to most agent evals.
relevance.action: Write one controlled scenario with ground truth for a stateful behavior in an existing agent, and track 3-4 separate metrics, including one guardrail, instead of a single pass rate.
